bib.title: Studying Large Language Model Generalization with Influence Functions

question: Which training sequences most influence an LLM's outputs, and what does that reveal about how LLMs generalise, when influence functions are scaled to models up to 52B parameters?
hypothesis: EK-FAC can approximate the inverse-Hessian-vector product accurately and cheaply enough to make influence functions usable on LLMs (stated as the approach; no hypothesis about the generalisation findings).
contributions: Use EK-FAC to approximate the IHVP for transformer LLMs up to 52B parameters, competitive with LiSSA and much faster
TF-IDF filtering and query batching (rank-32 compressed preconditioned query gradients) to cut training-gradient cost
Layerwise and tokenwise attribution of influence
Empirical study: sparsity/power-law tails, abstraction with scale, layerwise localisation, memorisation, word-order sensitivity, cross-lingual generalisation, role-playing

method.summary: Fits an EK-FAC approximation of the Gauss-Newton Hessian over the MLP layers of four pretrained decoder-only transformers (810M to 52B), then computes influence of pretraining sequences on the log-likelihood of a query completion, using TF-IDF-filtered candidates or unfiltered scans of 5-10M+ sequences with batched low-rank query gradients. Accuracy is validated against the proximal Bregman response function (PBRF) on small models and the 810M LM; findings are qualitative inspection of top sequences plus quantitative tail fits.
method.task: training data attribution via influence functions on pretrained LLMs

datasets.name: Pretraining distribution (512-token sequences)
datasets.size: unfiltered scans of at least 10 million sequences (about 5 million for the power-law fits); TF-IDF candidate sets of 10,000 sequences per query; 100,000 sampled sequences for the EK-FAC vs gradient dot product comparison
datasets.source: the models' pretraining corpus (not described in this paper)

datasets.name: Influence queries (about 50)
datasets.size: queries listed in Appendix E, Figs 42-47 (simple facts, math/programming/physics, memorised quotes, role-playing, translation, others)
datasets.source: hand-written; math queries from GSM8k (Cobbe et al. 2021); many derived from an Anthropic conversational assistant
datasets.preprocessing: coding queries use obfuscated variable names

datasets.name: UCI Concrete and Energy; MNIST; FashionMNIST; CIFAR10
datasets.source: public benchmarks used for PBRF validation
datasets.preprocessing: inputs normalised to zero mean, unit variance

other.extra: block-diagonal EK-FAC approximation with O=2 blocks per layer

models.name: Two-hidden-layer MLPs and ResNet-20
models.architecture: MLP 128 hidden Tanh (regression), 256 hidden ReLU (MNIST/FMNIST); ResNet-20 for CIFAR10

other.training: SGD batch size 128, grid search over L2 and lr

inference.samples: PBRF validation: 10 measurements/seeds with different test examples, 500 random training points; pseudo-gradient labels sampled from the model's output distribution to fit EK-FAC
inference.prompting: no prompting; queries are (prompt, completion) pairs, influence measured on f(theta) = log p(completion | prompt; theta); dialogue queries use 'Human: ... Assistant:' format
inference.retrieval: TF-IDF (modified Okapi BM25, k1 = 1.5), top 10,000 sequences per query; or unfiltered scan with query batching

parameters.layers_covered: MLP parameters of every layer; attention, embeddings, layer norm held fixed
parameters.sparsity_filter: drop tokenwise L2/L1 ratio above 2/3 as spurious
parameters.power_law_fit: MLE on top 0.01 percent of 5 million samples (500 sequences)
parameters.LiSSA_recursion_depth: number of data points, scaling tuned to avoid divergence

other.fine_tuned_models: not applied; influence computed on pretrained models only (Sec 5, footnote 1)

metrics.name: Pearson correlation with PBRF
metrics.definition: correlation of influence estimates with PBRF ground truth over 500 training points, averaged over 10 measurements

metrics.name: Influence
metrics.definition: change in log p(completion|prompt) from adding a copy of a training sequence; 1 = log-prob up by 1 nat

metrics.name: KS goodness-of-fit p-value
metrics.definition: Kolmogorov-Smirnov test of fitted power law, plausible if above 0.1 (Clauset et al. 2009)

eval.protocol: Validation vs PBRF on 5 datasets plus 810M LM; qualitative inspection of top sequences; synthetic training sequences scored by influence for word-order tests; Surge AI crowdworker summaries of 6 top sequences for 7 queries; no leave-one-out retraining (too costly).

evidence.quote: We consider four transformer language models from Kadavath et al. (2022), with approximately 810 million, 6.4 billion, 22 billion, and 52 billion parameters.
We set the layerwise damping factor as λℓ “ 0.1 ˆ meanpΛℓq for EK-FAC.
we use a block size of 2 (O “ 2) for the largest model investigated (the 52 billion parameter model)

results.claim: Flipping the order of English and Mandarin in influential training sequences reduces influence by at least an order of magnitude.
results.setup: english_to_mandarin query, 52B model, top influential English->Mandarin sequences re-ordered with identical content (Fig 26)
results.quote: when we flip the order of the English and Mandarin text in these sequences, the influence is reduced by at least an order of magnitude (and is possibly explainable as random noise for some), as shown in Figure 26.

results.claim: Worked English->Mandarin example: original order influence 0.116, flipped (Mandarin->English) 0.030, Mandarin-only 0.020.
results.setup: 52B model, english_to_mandarin query, one sequence modified from a top influential sequence (Fig 27); flipped 0.030; Mandarin-only 0.020
results.quote: The Mandarin-to-English sequence has an influence score of 0.030, which is similar to the score with a Mandarin-only sequence (0.020).
results.note: 0.116 appears in the Fig 27 heading 'English -> Mandarin Ordered Sequence (Influence = 0.116)'; 0.030 is only 3.9x lower than 0.116 for this single example, so the order-of-magnitude claim is about the Fig 26 set, not this example

results.claim: Synthetic fictional-fact sequences (Astrobia, Gleem): sequences with prompt-related phrase before completion-related phrase have consistently high influence; flipped order consistently lower.
results.setup: Queries 'The first President of the Republic of Astrobia was' -> 'Zorald Pfaff' and 'Gleem is composed of' -> 'hydrogenium and oxium'; 810M, 6.4B, 52B; synthetic sequences not in training set (Figs 24, 25)
results.quote: Sequences where phrases related to the prompt and phrases related to the completion appear in that order have consistently high influence. Sequences where the order is flipped have consistently lower influence.
results.note: Per-sequence influence values are bar plots (axis up to about 3.5 for Astrobia, 2.0 for Gleem) and are not in the text

results.claim: With flipped order, removing the prompt-related phrase does not change influence, so influence comes from the string Zorald Pfaff alone and the relation has not transferred.
results.setup: Astrobia query, synthetic sequence 'Zorald Pfaff was the first President of the Republic of Astrobia' (Fig 24)
results.quote: we observe that the influence is unchanged when the prompt-related phrase first President of the Republic of Astrobia is removed, suggesting that the influence comes from the string Zorald Pfaff, and that the model has not successfully transferred knowledge of the relation itself.

results.claim: Influence functions approximate sensitivity locally around the final weights and may miss nonlinear training phenomena; models might generalise across word orderings through nonlinear processes.
results.setup: Caveat attached to the word-order result
results.quote: Influence functions are approximating the sensitivity to the training set locally around the final weights (Bae et al., 2022a), and might not capture nonlinear training

results.claim: The Gauss-Newton Hessian linearises the parameter-output map so cannot model nonlinear coordination across parameter matrices such as induction-head formation.
results.setup: Discussion of EK-FAC / PBRF formulation
results.quote: The Gauss-Newton Hessian G linearizes the parameter-output relationship, so it is inherently incapable of modeling learning phenomena that require nonlinear coordination of multiple parameter matrices, such as the formation of

results.claim: Authors expect influence functions to fail to capture complex-circuit formation and global representation rearrangement.
results.setup: Upfront limitation
results.quote: We therefore expect they would fail to capture important nonlinear training phenomena such as the formation of complex circuits (Elhage et al., 2021) or global rearrangements of a model's representation (Power et al., 2022).
results.note: Source text uses a typographic apostrophe in model's

results.claim: EK-FAC reaches similar accuracy to LiSSA in at least an order of magnitude less time, and beats the gradient dot product, as measured by correlation with the PBRF.
results.setup: UCI Concrete/Energy, MNIST, FashionMNIST, CIFAR10 (ResNet-20), and the 810M LM; 500 training points; 10 measurements averaged (Figs 6, 7)
results.quote: EK-FAC achieves similar accuracy to the traditional iterative approach, but in at least an order of magnitude less time.
results.note: Correlation values are bar plots (Fig 6) and not in the text

results.claim: Influence tail follows a power law; the top 1 percent of sequences cover 12 to 52 percent of total positive influence on the 22B model.
results.setup: 8 queries, scan of 5 million unfiltered sequences, 22B model (Fig 9)
results.quote: for the 22B model, the top 1 percent of the sequences cover between 12 to 52 percent of the total influence for the queries we tested.

results.claim: Power-law exponent alpha fitted to the tail for shutdown is 2.28 (paperclips_large 2.1, water 2.57), so the standard deviation is infinite.
results.setup: Tail (top 0.01 percent among 5 million samples) of influence scores, 52B model
results.quote: the standard deviation of the power law fit to the queries paperclips_large (α “ 2.1), shutdown (α “ 2.28) and water (α “ 2.57) is infinite
results.note: Fig 8 panel labels print alpha = 2.21 (shutdown), 1.99 (paperclips_large), 2.87 (water), which differ from the text values

results.claim: Kolmogorov-Smirnov test rejects the power law for only 2 of 8 queries.
results.setup: Table 1 p-values; threshold 0.1 from Clauset et al. (2009)
results.quote: the KS test rejects the power law for only 2 out of 8 queries, indicating it is a reasonable fit for most queries.

results.claim: No query has any sequence with influence above 1; values above 0.1 are rare, so outputs result from many sequences collectively.
results.setup: 8 queries in Fig 8, 52B model; influence of 1 means log-prob of completion rises by 1 nat
results.quote: influence values larger than 0.1 are rare, and none of the 8 queries visualized have any sequences with influence larger than 1.

results.claim: About 5 million unfiltered sequences must be scanned to match the top-10 influence of TF-IDF filtered sets for most queries; at least 10 million were scanned.
results.setup: Estimated from fitted power laws
results.quote: for most queries, we estimated that scanning about 5 million sequences would be sufficient (Figure 8). For the sake of comprehensiveness, we scanned at least 10 million sequences for the rest of our experiments.

results.claim: Rank-32 approximation of preconditioned query gradients gives negligible error in influence estimates.
results.setup: 52B model, 8 queries, ranks 8 to 128 (Fig 3); correlation axis 0.875 to 1.0, shutdown correlation 0.995
results.quote: storing rank-32 approximations results in a negligible error in the final influence estimates, as shown in Figure 3.
results.note: Fig 3 panel label: shutdown (Correlation = 0.995) at rank 32

results.claim: Cross-lingual influence of English sequences on Korean/Turkish translated queries grows with model size; at 810M it is negligible.
results.setup: shutdown and water queries, 4 model sizes (Fig 16)
results.quote: For the smallest model, English training sequences have almost no influence on shutdown and water queries written in other languages. However, with increasing model scale, the cross-lingual influence of English sequences increases.

results.claim: Influence is spread roughly evenly across layers on average, but different query types concentrate in different layers: simple facts and memorised quotes in upper layers, math/code/translation in middle layers.
results.setup: Top 500 sequences for 50 queries (25,000 sequences), 52B model, layers in 9 blocks (Figs 17, 19)
results.quote: We computed the average layerwise influences from the top 500 influential sequences for 50 queries (a total of 25,000 influential sequences); as shown in Figure 17, for the 52B model, the influences were distributed nearly uniformly among the lower, middle, and upper layers of the network.

results.claim: Restricting influence to middle layers yields the most abstract generalisation patterns; lower/upper-only influence shows token overlap.
results.setup: superintelligent and inflation queries, 52B model, top 10,000 sequences from the original scans (Figs 20, 21)
results.quote: We found that limiting influence computation to the middle layers tends to yield the most abstract generalization patterns.

results.claim: Final-layer-only influence is likely to miss important patterns; all layers contribute distinctively.
results.setup: Contrasts with Koh and Liang (2017), Pruthi et al. (2020), Guo et al. (2021), Yeh et al. (2022)
results.quote: Our findings suggest that all layers of an LLM contribute to generalization in distinctive ways, and therefore influence function approximations limited to the final layer are likely to miss important patterns of influence.

results.claim: Influential sequences become more abstract and thematically related with model scale (810M, 6.4B, 22B, 52B).
results.setup: Queries trade, inflation, neurosemantic_facutitious, math_clips, binary_search, shutdown, paperclips, superintelligent
results.quote: While the influential sequences for smaller models tend to have short overlapping sequences of tokens, the top sequences for larger models are related at a more abstract thematic level

results.claim: Famous-quote queries return the exact passage as top influential sequences, showing the scan can detect clear memorisation; no clear memorisation found for typical outputs.
results.setup: Six famous-passage queries, unfiltered scan with query batching (Fig 22)
results.quote: we picked six queries that contain famous passages or quotes (which the AI Assistant is able to complete) and ran an influence scan over the unfiltered training data (i.e., using query batching rather than TF-IDF). We observed that invariably, the top influential sequences returned by our scan contained the exact famous passages.

results.claim: Role-playing (shutdown, paperclips, superintelligent) is supported as imitation of training text at a high level of abstraction; weak evidence against planning.
results.setup: 52B model top influential sequences
results.quote: Our results provide weak evidence against the hypothesis that role-playing behavior results from sophisticated agent representations and planning capabilities, but we are unable to rule out this hypothesis directly.

results.claim: Crowdworkers found a majority of the most influential sequences relevant to their queries.
results.setup: Surge AI; 6 top sequences for each of 7 queries at each model size
results.quote: Overall, the crowdworkers found a majority of the most influential sequences to be relevant to their corresponding queries.

results.claim: Influence calculation covers MLP parameters only; attention, embeddings and layer norm are held fixed.
results.setup: All experiments, all layers' MLP blocks
results.quote: we focus on computing influences only for the MLP parameters (Equation 23), treating the attention and other parameters (e.g., embeddings and layer normalization) as fixed.

results.claim: Influence analysis is on pretrained models only, not fine-tuned ones; fine-tuning analysis left as future work.
results.setup: All influence experiments
results.quote: our influence analyses focus on pretrained LLMs, so our experiments should be interpreted as analyzing which training sequences contribute to a response being part of the model's initial repertoire for the fine-tuning stage
results.note: Footnote 1 (p5): 'While the AI assistant was a fine-tuned model, our influence function computations focused on pretrained models.'

limits: Influence functions approximate the PBRF, local around final weights, not the leave-one-out counterfactual; authors expect them to miss nonlinear phenomena such as complex-circuit formation and global representation rearrangement (Sec 1) and say the Gauss-Newton Hessian cannot model induction-head formation (Sec 6).
The word-order insensitivity is shown for influence functions only; models might generalise across orderings through nonlinear processes not captured (Sec 5.3.4).
Pretrained models only; fine-tuning (and RLHF) not analysed. The assistant responses analysed came from a fine-tuned larger model than the four studied.
Models (up to 52B) are far smaller than state of the art; conclusions may not transfer to the full-size model.
Only MLP parameters are included; attention, embeddings, layer norm are fixed.
Only a fraction of the pretraining corpus is searched (5-10M sequences), so more influential sequences were likely missed; TF-IDF filtering biases results toward token overlap.
Whether the PBRF captures the training phenomena of interest is not addressed.

Tokenwise signs are hard to interpret; extremely sparse tokenwise influences may be algorithmic error or real; the top-1 percent coverage measure ignores negative influence and may understate concentration.
Findings are qualitative inspection of selected queries; no statistical test of the scale or layer-localisation claims; no code, compute or hardware stated.
Role-playing result is weak evidence only; influence spread over many examples could hide planning.

terms.definition: first-order Taylor approximation of the response function at epsilon = 0: I(z_m) = -H^-1 grad L(z_m, theta*)
response function to the proximal Bregman objective, which minimises loss on z_m while staying close to theta_s in function and weight space
Eigenvalue-corrected K-FAC: Kronecker eigenbasis from A and S, with diagonal eigenvalues fitted individually
share training-gradient computation across many queries by storing low-rank preconditioned query gradients in memory
